utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Both parties have announced that they had some preliminary matters to be raised. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Not at this moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- not --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I do, Your Honour, if I may, some sort of housekeeping matters first of all related to exhibits, because there's a fair number of them. First of all, yesterday I played a short clip from 65 ter number 33269, time code 8:06 to 8:16. That was a video from the school for the blind. It was MFI'd as P7605, and we've created a 65 ter number for that excerpt, which is 33269A. The clip has been burned onto a CD which we have, and could I now ask that 65 ter number 33269A be admitted, formally admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, no objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, P7605, the content now is found in 65 ter number 33269A. You have received the disk. P7605 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I also omitted to tender 65 ter number 33333, which was the unmarked version of the clip from this video, which -- the still, pardon me, not the clip, which Mr. Poparic then later marked. So if the unmarked version could be admitted, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry. Was 3333 not admitted as P7604?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Ah-ha. Absolutely. My mistake. Thank you. Now, with respect to D1336, which is a document my friend tendered, the statement of Huso Palo, admitted at T4 -- or I think admitted at T.40540, it was clear to me that this statement had been taken from part of the local investigative file for the incident, which Your Honours now have parts of in parts. And I thought, in the interests of effectiveness and having the context, fairness, that it would be prudent to use the whole investigative file which is now 65 ter number 33373; and I should also point out that in addition to subsuming D1336, this also subsumes P614, P615, P617, P618, and P619.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whether the -- if I could say so, the consolidated version, is that one that contains anything more than the -- the exhibits you have just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, it does. It contains other contemporaneous statements recorded at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Therefore, it's not just giving it a new --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- it's adding to it as well. Mr. Lukic, what's your position in relation to that because --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yeah, we should check. We could not object to having police file.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then what I would suggest is that you -- that you check it first and that we then take such action as suggested by Ms. Edgerton. And then perhaps also put it such a way that we're not later lost if we are trying to find, because the link with the other portions may easily be lost and we should take care that that doesn't happen. So I leave it at this moment. Suggestion is there. Mr. Lukic will look at. Mr. Lukic, shall we hear from you not later than by tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then another matter, Ms. Edgerton. Madam Registrar draws my attention to the fact that P7604 is the marked still of 33333. I don't know whether we need the unmarked still at all. Usually the marking doesn't take the view of what is under the marking, so therefore -- and it's usually sufficiently clear what the marking is and what the original photograph or the original still is. So if you wouldn't mind, then we leave it as it is. It's in evidence but the marked still.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. If I could deal with another document which we discussed yesterday, Your Honours. It's 65 ter number 10027, which is admitted under seal as P7614, and that relates to Scheduled Incident F-10. And 10027 are -- or is a collection of photographs that are part of the forensic file for this complete -- for the investigation, but I also realise 65 ter number 15704 is the complete investigative file for that incident, and also if I can just check the -- Mr. Poparic's report, I believe one of the -- includes some source material from Mr. Poparic's report. Your indulgence for a moment. Yes, indeed, I'm correct. 65 ter number 15704 includes document -- includes the photo file as I indicated yesterday and includes the material referred to at footnote 317 in Mr. Poparic's report, as well as, if I can go further, 311 and 315. So I don't know how this procedurally might work, Your Honour, but my recommendation would be - if it's at all possible - or my request would be to substitute 65 ter number 15704 for the document that was admitted as P7614 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: -- replacing that item with the whole investigative file.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's simpler than the previous one which was several. Any objections against --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think we should go through this document as well to see what that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. So we'll wait for a second. We'll hear from you not later than tomorrow, Mr. Lukic, before we decide on the request to have 65 ter 10027, which is admitted as P7614, to be replaced by 15704, which is the complete investigative report.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Only as I can see now, there are some documents in German so we might use help of Judge Fluegge. So I don't know what kind of compilation this is. We have to really go through the document carefully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do that and if you needs some German lessons, Judge Fluegge is available; and if he is not there, I might even assist you. We leave that until tomorrow as well. Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And a couple more, if I may, just all related to incidents we've discussed in the cross-examination so far, Your Honours. 65 ter number 33377 is the investigative file into the shooting of Adnan Kasapovic dated 24 October 1994, which was discussed -- which shooting was discussed yesterday, Your Honours, and is mentioned in Mr. Poparic's as well as Mr. Van der Weijden's report. And perhaps I can just go through the list because there's a couple more, if I may, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If we are -- it's all about full investigative reports replacing portions. Let me just -- I wasn't there yesterday, part of it, so let me just confer with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My colleagues tell me that at least 65 ter 33377 was not put to the witness in any way. If it is in his report, please guide us where it is to be found.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because then if it's footnoted somewhere in the report, it could be considered to be associated with the expert report.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And then what I would like to do, Your Honour, is come back to you on that more comprehensively at one time before the witness leaves the stand, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That would be more efficient I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the best would be if you make a kind of a table with all the relevant data, when or how it is to be linked to the testimony of the witness, either through his report or through his testimony. If it is his testimony, at what page it was; what was or is already admitted or marked for identification; what you suggest should replace that original document, so that we have a full overview and then can decide on it in a more organised way.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Perfect. Thank you. And the only other matter, Your Honour - and it's just by way of avoiding any surprises - as you know, I have been doing this a long time and I keep an eye on my time and I allotted for a extremely -- a generous cross-examination and I'm informed that I have one and a half hours left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's my information as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, this report - as Your Honours are aware - deals -- is a comprehensive one dealing with charged/uncharged, scheduled and unscheduled incidents. And while I apologise for not being accurate in terms of my anticipated time, I do have a concern at this moment that I may need more time, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You mean ten minutes or --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, if it was ten minutes I would do it a little bit closer to the end of my time. I think, Your Honours, based on things now, I might be making the exceptional -- the extraordinary request of an extra hour and a half. But that being said, Your Honours, of course I'll make every effort to move through more efficiently, keeping in kind the guidance that I have received from Your Honours over the course of these day. And I'd like to, at the end of this session, just update Your Honours with my time estimate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So that we are in a position to consider it during the break.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: One way or another, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Indeed, I think I yesterday reminded you that spending a lot of time on the wrong photograph is -- if it has no effect at all, then of course it's -- perhaps a bit of a credibility/reliability issue, but could have been limited in time because we didn't hear anything about any effect on the conclusions. Perhaps the best way to use our time is to get the witness into the courtroom. Ms. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, as you know, we never object if our friends from the opposite side need more time, but then I have to inform you that Mr. Poparic cannot finish tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Which means that how much time would you need in re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: By now, I have in between four and five hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll also consider that. Let's not forget that the reports presented by Ms. Subotic and Mr. Poparic are approximately 1.000 pages, which gives ample opportunity to address whatever one wants to address and -- so therefore, the Chamber - although giving some guidance as well - seven and a half hours is quite a lot. If we go to nine hours but then have another five hours then, that's -- we'll consider it, Mr. Lukic, but I leave to that at this moment, and we'll hear from Ms. Edgerton by the end of this session what her new time assessment is. We will ask the usher to escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The preliminary view of the Chamber is, Mr. Lukic, is that five hours for re-examination would be -- of course we do not know yet exactly what will follow in the next one and a half or two, two and a half, or three hours, but five hours it's likely that we will not allow the five hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, so many issues are raised --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- and I was directed to raise it in a re-direct examination, otherwise I would have to object all the time, get on my feet, interrupt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, at least organise your re-examination in such a way that you start with the most important matters, and then we're able to follow what level of importance and what level of relevance we are going through the -- so don't leave the most important and the most relevant questions for the end and the less relevant to start. Organise it in such a way that you convince us that it's really of great importance and great relevance and could not have been dealt with earlier. We leave it to that for the time being. Mr. Poparic, you had to wait for 20 minutes. Apologies for that. We'll now continue, and I remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony. Ms. Edgerton will now continue her cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Poparic.

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'd just like to deal very briefly with the incident we broke off dealing with - and that's incident F-8 - and take you right away to image 117 in your report and it appears between paragraphs 144 and 145. Now, you see your image 117. Now, I just want to ask one question before we begin. You didn't inspect - just to be perfectly clear - you didn't inspect the actual physical hole in the tram, just this one photograph; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Right. And yesterday, when you talked about bullets making perfectly round holes, I would -- I just want to understand the import of what you're saying. You're saying, is it your contention that bullets always make perfectly round holes?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Only if the impact is at an angle of 90 degrees. Any other angle produces an elliptical cross-section.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So you're -- it's -- you're saying that the distance from the target - the distance the bullet has to travel - has no effect on whether or not it makes a perfectly round hole; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not what I'm trying to say. I'm trying to say that the shape of the hole depends on the angle of impact, and the angle is also related to the distance, et cetera. It's part of the trajectory.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Does the shape of the hole depend on the velocity the bullet is travelling when it impacts?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We could say it does; but in this case, since the velocity is very high, we get a perfect imprint. I reminded you what high velocity means. When a bullet at high velocity hits glass, the glass is not shattered; that's why you get a good imprint.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So the shape of the hole depends on the velocity of the bullet?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this case, no, because the velocity is high. It's a specific case. We are not talking in general. If we are talking in general, then we can consider what you are saying; but in this specific case, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Does the shape of the hole depend on the bullet type?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, it depends on the size.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I didn't ask about the size of the bullet. I asked about the type of the bullet.

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, since a bullet is round in shape, in this case, I would say no.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So because bullets are round, they produce perfect holes if they're fired at high velocity; that's your position?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. My position is that the imprint on such a surface would be good even if the bullet is not round. Let's say that it had a star-like cross-section, the imprint would look like a star. I have cases when projectiles have wings and then you get the shape of wings on the imprint. It doesn't matter what the shape is. The shape remains the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And does the shape of the hole depend on the material the bullet impacts?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that much is true. If it's a soft material, for instance, canvas, the imprint would be less clear; but if it's a solid material, such as this tin sheet, then we get a very clear imprint.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And that tin sheet is material you didn't -- it's made of material you didn't analyse; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not analyse it and there was no need because I know the specifications of the tin that is used for this kind of product.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... you don't need to repeat yourself and you're repeating yourself from yesterday, so let me move on. So if -- even if we were to assume that bullets would make a perfectly round hole from a 90-degree angle, if they were entering from a 90-degree, angle - which I don't accept is accurate for a minute - but if we were to assume that, to conduct the type of analysis that you carried out in this case, you would have to take a photograph at a perfect 90-degree angle as well; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This photograph was taken at that angle, more or less, it was taken up close; and if there are any errors in terms of angle, they are very small. That is why I could analyse it well. It was the only case where a magnification of the hole existed. In other cases, such photographs were not available. This is the only case with a zoomed-in picture of a bullet.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Mr. Poparic. You're just saying that because you weren't there at the time this photograph was taken, you don't know the angle it was taken from, and all we've got in front of us is an enlargement. You have no idea what angle this photo was taken from, do you?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. I explained already. It was taken up close and could only have been taken from an angle very close to 90 degrees. Of course, I don't know it in absolute term, by the margin of error is very low.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Poparic --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... otherwise we'll have -- we'll go for days. The witness has the right to answer the question the best way he knows how to. He cannot be told how to answer the question. He has to be let to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, let's ... in general terms, I would agree with you. To say that you would need more days, Mr. Lukic, on the basis of just this may go a bit far. Witness, you said it was taken up close and could only have been taken from an angle very close to 90 degrees and that you don't know it in absolute terms but that the margin of error is very low. What would you want to add to that which seems to be an answer to the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think I said it all. The error is small, and I've already explained how the photograph was taken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, there's also -- Ms. Edgerton is also bound by time, so if she has received an answer to her question, often where the witness has an inclination to go well beyond that, it is not under all circumstances impermissible to interrupt the witness. Witness, could you tell us if it would be -- well, let's say, not 90 degrees but 80 degrees, what would be approximately the oval -- what would be the distortion compared to a full circle, do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There would be some kind of deformation of the circle, albeit it small; I don't know to which side, though. It is very important to which side the angle is turned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I interrupted you because you were not giving an answer to my question. Apparently you do not know exactly how it would change, in centimetres or millimetres, the shape of the hole.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As regards the size itself, the difference would be very small, although I can't tell what you it would be off the top of my head. In any case, there would be a very small deformation to the circle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Would you also agree that if there is a possible margin of error in how you put the circles in the -- on the photograph, if you move it just a few millimetres, it would still be more or less the black hole, isn't it? There's some margin of appreciation there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct. I did bear that in mind. I based my conclusion on the difference related to the direction that is alleged as the trajectory of the projectile, and the right angle - and the difference taken into account - allowed ne to draw my conclusions to sufficient degree of accuracy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, again you're not answering my question, but I leave it to that. Ms. Edgerton. Judge Fluegge would have a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I'm sorry for that. You said, I quote: "It was taken up close and could only have been taken from an angle very close to 90 degrees." What is the factual basis of your knowledge that this was taken have a close distance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had the photograph that I used. It comes from the photograph. In my assessment, it was taken at a distance of 50 or 60 centimetres, so quite up close. One could see the hole very well, and it was obviously the intention of the photographer to show the shape of the hole.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Do you know which camera was used?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we just go one page earlier in both languages in Mr. Poparic's report, please, to image 116.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And you see it on the right-hand side of the page in front of you, Mr. Poparic.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we just blow up the English page, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That's the photograph you're talking about, isn't it, Mr. Poparic? That's the photograph you enlarged to make the image that appears as 117 in your report; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Oh, fine [Microphone not activated] --

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I referenced the photograph in question.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So, Mr. Poparic, we don't have the report -- we don't have the photograph -- we don't even have the photograph you enlarged to make your image 117, do we? It's not in your report?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, that's a question, I take it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not in the report itself, but it is referenced. It was an exhibit from the Galic case; that is where I found the photograph. I would have never been able to do this on the basis of the photograph you showed; it would take much magnification and it wouldn't be clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Poparic, let's move on then and thank you, you've answered my question. I'd like to go on to incident F-11 which is at page 188 in your report in English and B/C/S page 183, paragraphs 171 to 192. So this is an incident, Mr. Poparic, where -- and it took place on the 8th of October, 1994, and it's an incident that involves the targeting of two trams within minutes of one another and pedestrians. And your contention is that the origin of fire in all three incidents was a shooter in the Executive Council building and not from anywhere in VRS-held territory; is that fair?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, your position is based on a number of things: Dust clouds on a bit of film; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Glass shards on another bit of film?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: A bit of film on which General Rose appears?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Rather than getting into an argument of what bit we're talking about, I'll just move on and we'll come back to this. The angle of fire as measured by UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And the position of a man who was killed riding in tram 206? I've covered just about everything now; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. Let's deal first with the dust clouds --

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And if I may add, witness statements.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Poparic, the more you add without me asking you, the longer you're going to stay here. So let's talk about dust clouds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, that was unfair because you put two questions and he was waiting for the translation of the questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Oh.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And this second question you put to the witness he addressed in his answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I accept that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Poparic, it's correct that you admitted in your Karadzic testimony that your dust cloud analysis isn't based on any published studies or trials; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not based on the results of published studies, but these are some general principles of the strike theory. I don't know what your interpretation of it may be, but I have never claimed that the method was unreliable.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And I'm just going to ask you about what you said in the Karadzic case. And when we asked you this in the Karadzic case, this very same question, your answer was, at pages 39252, 19 to 21, 65 ter 32790, page 90, your answer was: "A. It is based on experience. I see no reason for conducting a study. It would be irrelevant." That was your evidence in the Karadzic case; do you stand by it?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. What I had in mind was my experience, which is very extensive, and I know what kind of dust trail is left at a sharp angle as opposed to other angles - I have seen it countless times - however, as I said already, I also base it on the strike theory.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, I'd like to briefly pay attention to the transcript where Judge Fluegge intervened, because otherwise it may be very difficult to understand. I think that when you put the question to the witness: "All right. Let's deal first with the dust clouds --" That it was then the witness who said: "And if I may add, witness statements." And he rightly did so because you suggested to him that you had dealt with every source, and therefore it was totally appropriate for the witness to add this because he corrected a suggestion which was wrong. But I think it should be clear on the transcript that it was not your question in which it was said: "And if I may add, witness statements" but it was the witness who introduced that. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely accepted.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, in terms of your experience that you've just talked about, it's correct that you also testified in the Karadzic proceedings that your experience is with level trajectories; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And there's no citations in your report to any publications that deal with -- or that detail what conclusions we could draw from the shape and size of dust clouds by a bullet striking the ground, are there?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So you're just asking us to take your word for it that this necessitates the conclusion that the bullets in this case hit the ground at a high angle of descent; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is rather difficult to answer it with a yes or no because I don't fully agree with this assertion. I do not assert that you have to take my word for granted. I thought it was well explained why it should be taken into account, at least in my view.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I just want to move on to the shards of glass. Now you told the Judges in your testimony in-chief that shards of glass or the shards of glass shattered on the ground by this tram were evidence that the tram was hit at that place where we saw the glass on the ground. Now you've spent a little bit of time today explaining your testimony yesterday which was that glass doesn't shattered when it's pierced by a bullet, and maybe you need to explain why -- and I'll read you exactly what you said yesterday. You said: "When it pierces the glass, the velocity" -- actually, no, let me go earlier. Referring to F-8 you talked about the speed of the projectile and the homogeneity of the material. And you said: "So it's out of the question. The best example is glass. When it pierces the glass, the velocity is such that the glass is not shattered." So putting your testimony yesterday against your earlier evidence about the glass shards, you contradict yourself; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I can explain.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I think you should explain the contradiction. Would you like to do that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Or to explain whether there's no contradiction, Ms. Edgerton --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Accepted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- please try to -- it's the witness who testifies. Please proceed. Can you please explain.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I mentioned glass in the previous case, I mentioned it because there are great differences in terms of material between glass and steel, plus there are different types of glass. There are numerous examples of rifle bullets flying through glass panes without the pane being shattered, with only a hole left behind that projectile. That is why I said that there are such cases where the glass is not shattered but, rather, intact with some cracks around the hole. It doesn't mean, though, that it will not shatter later, especially because in this specific case we don't know when it happened and perhaps there could have been two bullet, the other one shattering the pane. It is not mandatory that the pane wouldn't shatter, but there are many cases where bullets fly through the glass, leaving just a very clear hole with cracks. On the other hand, I do not try to say that a glass pane not shatter if hit by a bullet, so neither is mandatory. It doesn't have to shatter as a must.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So you've just said that there are cases where, when glass is hit by a bullet, that it could shatter later; yet you pointed out to the Trial Chamber that the evidence of the shards of glass shattered on the ground beside the tram were indisputable evidence that the tram was hit at the place where we saw the grass [sic]. Now, in fact, based on what you've just said, we can't exclude the possibility that the glass could have been hit somewhere other than where you say the tram stopped?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was hit at that spot, and I can explain why, with your leave. We've already discussed it during examination-in-chief, but I can explain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps in your explanation you focus on what was put to you by Ms. Edgerton. Ms. Edgerton says: You told us that the shattering may occur later, therefore how could you conclude for certain that the shattered glass indicates where the shot was fired because it could have been earlier? That's the question. If would you explain that to us, not why - otherwise - your conclusions are right or wrong but that element. Please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will try. We've touched upon that in examination-in-chief. I said that I base my conclusion on witness statements, and the witnesses said that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm stopping you there, because that may be other good reasons to draw your conclusions. Please focus on the matter which was raised. We are not inviting you to defend your final conclusions. You were asked a question about what conclusions you can draw alone from finding the shattered glass there, in view of your testimony that sometimes it shatters immediately, sometimes it does later, and sometimes it just leaves a hole. That's the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this case, it shattered and fell on the ground next to the tram where it was stopped.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which leaves the question: Why? Where you said sometimes it shatters, why you could conclude that in this case it shattered immediately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because the shards are next to the tram.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think that somebody shattered the glass subsequently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, nevertheless you testified that sometimes it shatters after the impact and not immediately at the time of the impact. But please proceed, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And also in your examination-in-chief, talking about this incident at transcript page 40511 to 40512, you said -- you referred to the UNPROFOR reports about the incident and you said: "In the grass they found six craters and managed to put antenna of radio equipment there, and that shows that the angle was also much bigger than the one that was possible if fire had come from positions of the VRS. If that had a been the case there would have only been a shallow furrow. An antenna couldn't stick into it. Practically it would fall on the ground." So your position is if the shot in this case came from VRS-held territory, the projectiles would have come in at a shallow angle; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I would like to play a very short bit of film in that regard now, please now, P784 and I think it might be even less than a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we do so, if you say, "very shallow angle," where do you think an angle is still shallow and where -- what makes -- is that 30 degrees? 20 degrees? 15? 40? Where do you make it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this case it is below 10 degrees. The highest degree that could have been achieved from VRS positions was 5.71 degrees at house number 12, as marked by UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Again, you're not answering my question, unfortunately. I didn't ask you what -- what -- what the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Below 10 degrees, as I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You say it's shallow if it's below 10 degrees?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you say "shallow," do you mean a low angle, a small angle? Let me try to be clear because I'm confused about the interpretation. If the angle is below 10 degrees, the furrow will be shallow, the trace left will be shallow; that's what I wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We leave it to that for the time being. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. And I should note we're not going to play P784 with any sound. If we could play it, it begins at time code -- oh.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Stop, at time code 46:7.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: These -- this is film of the UNPROFOR officers doing their analysis with the antenna. I'm just going to ask that we back up a couple of seconds and then continue and then I'm going to ask you a question.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That film of UNPROFOR doing their line-of-sight analysis with the antenna shows that there was only a shallow furrow. The antenna, just like you said it was, would -- was practically falling into the ground. That shows an angle consistent with fire from VRS-held territory, doesn't it, according to your own analysis?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this footage I cannot estimate the angle at which the antenna is set, but I maintain that if the bullet came in at an angle of 5 degrees, it's absolutely impossible for it to land in that hole.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I see it's break time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is. We'll take a break. We'd like to see you back in 20 minutes. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll resume at ten minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would like to interrupt before the witness is with us. I have two translation issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At page 20, line 3, the witness mentioned --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Shall the witness wait outside the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, may be better.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be -- Mr. Poparic, could you, one second.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's nothing major but then it can be checked with Mr. Poparic. So here, page 20, line 3, he said: "There are great differences in terms of material between glass and steel ..." After this comma, he said: "... unlike metal glass is amorphous material," and then it goes "plus ..." Obviously there was something that was before, so that could be checked with him and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It's a question if the transcript is correct and not a translation issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I don't -- I didn't hear that it was translated, so whatever was translated is entered in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I will try to deal with it in a quick way.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. And then page 24, line 8, in this sentence: "It's absolutely impossible for it to land in that hole." It appears that it's addressing the bullet, but actually what witness was addressing is antenna. So it's -- then it should be: "It's absolutely impossible for it to be placed in that hole." So I would like you to check with him. Because he was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. We'll check both items. Could the witness be escorted in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, we briefly discussed in your absence a few possible errors in translation or transcription. I go with you through them. First, I read part of an answer as it was translated and transcribed. It was about -- I read it: "I mentioned it because there are great differences in terms of material between glass and steel, plus there are different types of glass." Is there anything in what I just read to you, what is missing from your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot remember whether it's in that sentence, but I meant the difference in homogeneity of material between glass and metal. And I said glass is amorphous, which means that it's structure is not always equal in all parts. That was the essence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that was, indeed, the issue raised. Then I would like to take you another part, and I read the answer as it was translated and transcribed for us. You said: "In this footage, I cannot estimate the angle at which the antenna is set, but I maintain that if the bullet came in at an angle of 5 degrees, it's absolutely impossible for it to land in that hole." Is there any correction you'd like to make to what I just read to you? And perhaps you focus on the last part of what I read.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This conclusion is correct. I didn't -- I can't remember whether I said 5 or 5.71 about the angle at which it was possible to fire a bullet from the positions of the VRS. I don't know if I said 5.71, but that's basically it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you'd focus on the last, and I repeat that portion: "... it's absolutely impossible for it to land in that hole ... " Is that what you said and did you -- and could you explain what you meant by "it"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it's impossible for the furrow to be such as to set the antenna there. It had to be a shallow furrow, and then the antenna could not be placed in it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I think we've dealt with it. Ms. Edgerton, you may now proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, the film that we just saw, P784, before we broke, includes, Mr. Poparic, images that you included in your report at page 199 as image 149 - and you did that without actually citing to a specific piece of film - but there you say that these images depict UNPROFOR member pointing out a detailing on the BiH Executive Council building to General Michael Rose. Now in the Karadzic case, you can confirm that in the Karadzic case, when you first listened to this film, it had no soundtrack, right, because that's what you said in the Karadzic case?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So you also confirmed that your assertion that an UNPROFOR member is pointing out a detail on the Executive Council building is just an assumption?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's no assumption. He was showing a shape and pointing at the building. It's just one action that I noticed in the footage. I did not make any claims on the basis of that and I didn't assume anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: P670, which is the UNPROFOR report -- leaving the video aside. P670, which is the UNPROFOR report that you spent a lot of time on in your analysis, has no mention of anyone in UNPROFOR suspecting that the shots came from the Executive Council building. You saw that, so you would agree? There's not a single mention in that report of the shots coming from the Executive Council building?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton does not allow translation to finish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the proper way of saying is: Could Ms. Edgerton please wait until -- rather than to use an angry voice. There's no reason for that. At the same time, Ms. Edgerton --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- it's true, slow down. Wait for the translation to be finished.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. If that number denotes the video we saw before, I didn't have the opportunity to see it. I saw a movie which contains some parts of it and others not. For instance, I had not seen before the part with the antenna. And in the movies that I saw, there was no sound; I wasn't able to hear anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So you never saw film of UNPROFOR with the antennas before making your assertions about the angle at which they would have hit the ground; is that what I understand you to say? Can you just tell me if I have that right?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you did not. I talked about the video, P670, in general. I didn't have the footage filmed by UNPROFOR. I had the opportunity to see a compilation of sorts which doesn't have all of these segments. I had never seen the antennas or the whole report about the antennas.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now the male victim whose profile you draw in your report at your page 197, image 147, is the next thing I want to turn to. And in respect of that, I just want to get you to confirm your testimony in the Karadzic case in relation to that man. It's correct, isn't it, that you specifically acknowledged that if his position was different from your assumption that he was sitting or standing at the time he was hit, that the -- your argument that the shots -- according to which the shots were fired from the Executive Council building would be brought into question. Can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. I'd like to show you your testimony in the Karadzic case.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: 65 ter number 32788, please, it was on the 30th of May, 2013. Can we go over to e-court page 53, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So here you said, talking about this incident and this man, to His Honour Judge Morrison the following. He said: "Just one matter --" that's at line 3 at page 39019. "Just one matter. I mean, that assumption is predicated on the basis that the victim was in a vertical or near-vertical position at the time of the impact on the ground [sic]. If he had, for instance, been leaning over at the time of the impact of the round, the [sic] assumption wouldn't stand, would it?" And you responded: "[As read] That is correct. He was leaning over, that is correct, can be called into question." Are you prepared to -- do you stand by the testimony you gave to His Honour Judge Morrison in the Karadzic case?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, but I don't think your question is fair because I did not deal with that in my report. I should like to be allowed to explain how --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, first of all, the question was whether you stand by what you said in the Karadzic trial. That is a question which is fair; no question about that. Then there was one minor thing, however, Ms. Edgerton. I heard you read what is transcribed to us: "He was leaning over, that is correct ..." What he said and what we find in the transcript is: "If he was leaning over, that is correct ..." You misread there.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, listen carefully to Ms. Edgerton's next question. If there's anything unfair in what was asked from you at the time of your Karadzic testimony, then Mr. Lukic certainly will -- I take it you have drawn his attention to that or that he can deal with that if need be. Please proceed, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So you have no idea what position this man was in at the moment he was shot, do you?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We cannot hear what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your answer and speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I do have a picture.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No, my question to you relates to the man's position at the moment he was shot. It's correct, isn't it, he could have been crouching, turning, talking, even lying on the floor at the moment he was shot. We have no evidence of what he was actually -- how he was actually positioned at the moment he was shot, do we?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we have data. We have information and evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Are you trying to say that the picture on which you based your drawing in your report is that evidence?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's get to the point. What is there you know now about the position of the man? Is that statements? Is that anything else? Could you clearly -- not conclusions, et cetera, but just what information do you have which is not yet in the report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That information is in the report, but I can say it. First of all, we have the information in which part of the body he was hit and where the bullet ended up, and we have an image of the tram where the man was injured, it's tram 206, it's the first one. And based on the traces of blood in that tram - in one video we have seen today - we see where he could have been, in the front part of the tram. And there are only two locations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll stop you there. It's not an answer to the question. The question is not where he was but how he was positioned, lying up, et cetera. And you say: Where you could have been. We're not interested in analysis of where he could have been -- we may be interested in that, but if you could tell us what exactly the information is on which you think you can determine, or what this Chamber can determine, what the position of this victim was, lying, standing, bending over, whatever.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was standing, and that's indicated by the damage inside the tram. In no other position could he have been injured the way he was. The glass is intact. There are some traces -- there are no traces below the seat, and the only thing consistent with his injuries is that he was standing and there are some traces of blood on the side of the tram inside, which indicates that he was standing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And with respect to incident F-16 in your report, which is incident F-15 in this indictment, and it's at B/C/S page -- it begins in a section at B/C/S page 232, English page 239. Just like the case of this man, your argument is predicated on the basis that the victim was taking a certain position. Now, your argument is predicated on the basis that Mr. Agovic was sitting facing directly forward in his seat at a 45-degree angle vis-à-vis the tram. So when I -- and you confirmed that to me in the Karadzic case at e-court page 32790 -- pardon me. 65 ter number 32790, e-court pages 78 to 79. You said: "It's assumed that his sitting position was normal." So your point, your position, your argument, wouldn't be valid if Mr. Agovic's body had been angled a bit to the left or a bit to the right, would it?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As to a little bit to the left or a little bit to the right, that has been analysed and the conclusion would remain the same. As for the assumptions you mentioned, these are all facts that are in the -- the case file.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If Mr. Agovic had been bending over, if he had been turning, if he had been talking, your argument with respect to the angle of fire in this incident comes into question, just like the incident we've just finished with. Because you've just said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Wait for the translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Oh. I apologise. I thought I was. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All the witness statements, including Mr. Agovic's, indicate that he was not even making any movements, he was not bending or anything. If you have any specific information, then we can discuss what positions those could have been. We cannot talk like this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, could I ask you: If you say, if someone is not saying in a statement that he was bending over, then you take it for a fact that he was not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Even if the person had been bending, in view of the height at which he was hit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Witness, would you please answer my question. My question was: If someone in a statement doesn't say that he was bending over, you take it for a fact that he was not bending over?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And I just want to skip over -- actually, I'd like to ask you one more question about this incident. Your report shows you had a look at the criminal investigation file for this incident. Now, so that you --

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So then you would know that this report emphasises the fact that other trams immediately behind this one were fired on from the same Serb positions and immediately afterwards there was an exchange of fire between UNPROFOR and this position - and that's at P612, English page 8; B/C/S page 7. So having looked at the investigative file, you saw that?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw that stated and I had no other information, but I didn't base my analysis on what was happening around. I based it on the possibility that the tram was hit as alleged from the positions said, so I analysed all the traces that were sufficient for me to make this analysis.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So you -- what you're saying is you didn't think the evidence that UNPROFOR responding to the alleged origin of fire in VRS-held territory was relevant to your analysis; that's what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't going to say that. I wanted to say that I did not have information. It was stated by a witness who was not in the area but she only heard an exchange of fire, and there was a French UNPROFOR member apparently who was wounded. On the basis of that statement, I don't know where that exchange of fire was and I would have to speculate. It was stated as such, though, but I based my conclusions on my analyses on the basis of the traces left. I don't know what happened before or later. I cannot relate that to the case. I have no information that would make me establish a connection between the two or even three incidents. I don't know how many there were exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'd like to move on to incident F-14 in your report which is F-13 in this indictment, and the section in your report that that deals with begins at English page 225, B/C/S page 218, paragraphs 209 to 218. Now if we can just go over to your image 164, which is I think at English page 221 and -- pardon me, B/C/S page 221; English page 228. Thank you. Now you say in the caption of this report without citing to any part of Huso -- pardon me, the caption to this image without citing to any part of Huso Palo's testimony per se, you say that the circle that says tram 263 is the position of the tram according to his evidence. But you know that -- but you know that that's not where Huso Palo says the tram was, don't you? In fact --

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that Huso Palo said that the tram was at that location. He clearly stated that as he was about to go across the intersection, he could hear it - the fork, that is to say, for the tram, that Huso Palo testified about.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Poparic, Huso Palo, in his statement given to the police on 24 November 1994, which is 65 ter number 1D00691, states that the tram was hit when he reached the section between the technical school and the Marsal Tito barracks, specifically turning towards the railway station. In his statement P162, dated February 24, 1996, he says that the tram was hit between the technical school and the Marsal Tito barracks. And then in his testimony in the Dragomir Milosevic case, in 1D05751, he says that the tram was fired at between the two museums. None of that evidence puts tram 263 at the location where you marked it. In fact, according to the evidence of Huso Palo, tram 263 was further east in the intersection, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The first two statements he provided that were available to me indicate that spot. As for what he said in his testimony, I did not have it at my disposal. It is further towards the east, that is correct; but the first two statements are precisely at the location where I indicated, perhaps not to the metre, but that is the intersection.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, in fact, the effect of the difference between whether the tram is in the intersection or not, the effect of it puts the tram in better view of four white sky-scrapers in Grbavica where you agreed there were VRS sniping positions, and that's what Mr. Palo's evidence does?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there are two issues here. If it is correct that the tram was where he put it in his testimony, he was not visible from the white high-rises, as we could see in the photograph you showed yesterday. He was then at the Holiday Inn and visible from the Metalka building, and I treated it in my report. In that case, it was visible from the Metalka building and not from the white high-rises. If he was at the intersection as I marked, according to his two statements provided previously, then it was visible from the white high-rises but not from the Metalka building. That is the only difference; however, I treated both scenarios in the report.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: One --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you one question. You said in one of your previous answers: "It is further towards the east, that is correct." When did you learn that it was further to the east, which you now say is correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The testimony of Huso Palo, I learned about it now, but there are other testimonies indicating the place he pointed out. I had learned that previously and that is why -- and analysed both tram positions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So I do understand that while Ms. Edgerton was reading to you a statement that you never had -- oh, his testimony, you never heard about that before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had not heard that testimony of his previously, but I did hear the testimony of others, that he was at the place he indicated. Therefore, I was aware of the two positions, and I analysed them both in the report. There's no dispute.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We can get exact citation from the transcript, since we want to check it and it's not read from the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there's any doubt about that, Ms. Edgerton, you're invited to read literally from the transcript. If you did not -- and if you did, please give the reference to Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I didn't read exactly, but I can certainly give the page and line reference. It's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And would you then also read it -- if you did not read it exactly, could you then please read it exactly so that we have an opportunity to verify that now.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It's at 1D05751, please, e-court page 3, lines 14 to 17 Mr. Palo says: "I remember the date. I remember the date that I read. On that day, I drove a tram between Marin Dvor and the technical school and the Marsal Tito barracks. I was fired at between the two museums. On the left there were the four sky-scrapers and there was firing."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, that's at least one of the sources which is pretty accurate, I would say, as far as between the two museums.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps during the next break if you need further references then we don't need to spend time on it in court, unless there's any accuracy and then, of course, we would --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, but we have to have a reference to be able to check. I wouldn't raise --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, but that's the reason why I -- this was an open invitation to Ms. Edgerton to give you those references for the other sources she mentions, and then can you check it. And if there's any problem, we'll hear it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And Ms. Edgerton referred earlier to the document, the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But not the page, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, as precise as possible, Ms. Edgerton, for Mr. Lukic so that he can always verify.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll always do my best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Just one last thing with respect to this incident is --

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. I apologise, if I may, since I was answering the question as the testimony of this person was read out, he said that he was at the location I indicated. He did not change it. He said between the two museums, one of them being the museum of the revolution, the other one being the national museum. He confirmed the location; it is just that he described it differently. That location is identified in image 164 of my report. You can look at image 164, the two musea are marked with 3 and 4, and he stated that the tram was between the two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Which doesn't allow any plotting. It could be anywhere between the two, isn't it? Could be further to the east as well. It is still between number 3 and number 4 on your sketch, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct. Then it would be visible from the four high-rises but not visible from the Metalka building. That is the gist of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but you just don't know. It's just between the two, between 3 and 4, and you put it somewhere arbitrary.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Around there, approximately. That is how I indicated it and analysed it. What I'm trying to say is that he did not testify differently to that, but he confirmed it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You've answered my question. And may I take it that 263 and 263 [sic] as we find it on the sketch is some kind of an error. On the plotting, it is 263; in the legenda, it is 236.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is a mistake. It was copied from elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, let's try to avoid mistakes. Please proceed, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: One more hopefully short area with respect to this incident. You said in your testimony in-chief that given their position and their detailed explanations and given the description of their wounds - and that's referring to the two victims - that they could only have been hit if the bullet came through the joint of the articulated tram, the soft part; but in that case, it would not have come from the building of the Executive Council of Bosnia and Herzegovina and not from the Metalka or the high-rises, irrespective of the tram's location. Now, and I just want to focus on Mrs. Karacic, one of the victims in this regard. During your cross-examination in the Karadzic case, you confirmed you had never seen the entry or exit wounds Mrs. -- the injuries Mrs. Karacic suffered that day. Can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness kindly repeat his sentence. We did not understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you repeat your sentence. You were not understood.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not see the wound, but I did see a report indicating where the entry and exit wounds were.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And can you also confirm that in the Karadzic case you agreed there were no measurements in the official report showing the vertical distance the bullet fragment travelled inside her arm?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. There's only a general description.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I give some guidance both at this moment to you, Ms. Edgerton, and also later to you, Mr. Lukic. At various moments several times this Chamber pointed at the fact that this witness is doing our job assessing/evaluating the evidence, et cetera, et cetera. Now by focussing so much on all which is beyond his expertise, you are taken by the witness rather than to stick to what this witness could tell us, and that is what is within his expertise. I'm afraid that happened quite a bit during examination-in-chief, it happens in cross-examination as well, and it may have all been triggered by the way the witness deals with such matters in his report. But I think we are the ones -- the lawyers know where the limits are of expert evidence, and if you would stick to that more strictly, then that would certainly shorten some of the time. And perhaps it shouldn't have been there already from the beginning, but that's too late to establish at this moment. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. And now I want to move over to F-12 which is at English page 210, B/C/S page 204, and paragraphs 193 to 208.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now -- and this is the incident dealing with Mrs. Sokolovic and her son Nermin. Now you would accept that if the mother and boy who were shot in this case were standing at the zebra crossing at the intersection of Zmaja od Bosne and Franje Rackog at the moment they were shot, they would have been visible with the naked eye as civilians to any shooter in the Metalka building. You'd accept that, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on all the material shown to me --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- I analysed --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I don't want to hear about the material. Mr. Poparic, I want to hear, based on -- Mr. Poparic.

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: -- I want to hear - based on your experience and whatever expertise you might have and from your personal visits to the area - whether you'd accept that if they were standing at the location I said, they would be visible with the naked eye as civilians to any shooter.

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If they were standing at the place alleged, they would have been visible. That is not something I disputed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And at a distance -- and you -- you would agree with me that Metalka building is about 300 metres from the location I've just described; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And at a distance of 300 metres, the victims in this case were targets that were easily attainable with one well-aimed shot from the Metalka building, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A good shooter could make that hit.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now just in terms of the thrust of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see -- your microphone was open as is mine now but I can't hear anything through our earphones. And I think it's now okay again. Please resume.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now just in terms of thrust of your argument, I want to deal with two points, and that's your assertion that Sokolovic and her son were hit in a cross-fire, and you say that in paragraph 204; and that the boy was shot in a different location, and you say that at paragraph -- English page 290, B/C/S page 271.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I think I've got those pages right.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So just with respect to the first point about the cross-fire. You can confirm, can't you, that -- I'd like you to confirm your evidence in the Karadzic case that anything you saw -- no, let me rephrase that, if I may. In terms of the cross-fire, you specifically accepted that you could have been referring to UNPROFOR's anti-sniping team's responding to the source of fire in this incident, right, and not cross-fire between the warring factions?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't think you stated what I said properly. I simply registered that in his statement she said that once she approached the municipal building, shots were heard and people fell to the ground. I was not discussing any exchange of fire. As for what you said about the anti-sniping team, you put it to me in my Karadzic testimony, but that happened afterwards. And then, based on what you read out to me, I could not confirm where the shooting occurred. It was a simple daily report by UNMO, no direction of fire was indicated in the document. Therefore, I exclude the possibility of an exchange of fire between UNPROFOR and someone else, because I simply did not have such data. You put to me later on that there was a report showing that UNPROFOR intervened on the day, but I didn't see where or in what direction. There was just some very general information.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Let's have a look at that UNPROFOR report.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It's 65 ter number 11215.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, whether there was fire or not is a factual matter for which we do not need expert evidence. I think we -- yesterday or the day before yesterday we had lengthy discussions about if you hear shots fired that it's important to know whether it happened immediately after the incident or before that, but even that is not something which falls within the expertise of this witness. It is just dealing with a few matters where he went out, where he started interpreting all the evidence. Now we hear that he had looked at this but he hadn't available that -- and that's, of course, not what really matters at this moment. I would have a very short question to you. In paragraph 204, when you say that what you saw on the video, that that indicates that fighting was going on at the time and that fire was being exchanged between the warring parties, are you referring to any firing you heard in that video which preceded the incident?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If the footage is accurate, it is something that happened later, but the video is a compilation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- it should be afterwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Therefore, it doesn't say anything about any exchange of fire before that. Second, if you hear shots being fired and if you conclude that there is an exchange of fire, what is there that makes you so sure that it's a fire exchange between the warring parties and not any other party?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't say there was an exchange of fire. I did not analyse the footage. I just wanted to show that something could be heard --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Witness, I stop you there and take to you paragraph 204. You are describing that in the video that what you hear and what you see, and you said which indicates that fighting was going on at the time and that fire was being exchanged between the warring parties. As far as the time is concerned, you have now confirmed that it must have been after the incident. Now how can you hear if you hear a shot, who fires it, and whether it's from the warring parties?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this paragraph, I only indicate what I could hear on the footage because it seems that there was some --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... and I asked you: How can you hear that the shots you hear are part of an exchange of fire between the warring parties? That's my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is only an assumption, but I did not rely on it when analysing the case. It was just a statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. I think can I deal with one more incident hopefully before the break very quickly.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It's F-3 in Dobrinja, Mr. Poparic. And just -- and the way I want to deal with that is this: In your report, you specifically accepted that SRK forces manned and maintained observation posts in the tower of the church in Veljine, and that was based on a document I showed you during your cross-examination in Karadzic and I need to show you the document now.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It's P2389.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So two-thirds of the way down the first page in your language - and by the way, this is an Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina intelligence report of the 5th Motorised Battalion dated 2 October 199 -- pardon me, 5th Motorised Brigade dated 2 October 1993. So about two-thirds of the way down the first page and at the English page 2 at the top of the page, there's a paragraph that says: "The enemy uses the church at Veljine exclusively as an observation post. According to our information till now in the church there are six observers per shift. The observers are armed with snipers and one PAM which is in a well-fortified nest in the church. From the church, fire is rarely building opened, and when it is opened, a sniper with a silencer are used." These are exactly the types of weapons you identified last week as being able to target the victim in this incident, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could have, but it's not the only weapon that could have fired that particular shot. I didn't say it was the only one.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No, I didn't ask you about these being the only ones, but you've answered the question now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And I think that takes us to the break, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'd like to see you back in 20 minutes from now. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, you promised that you would give us a better insight in the time you would still need by the end of this session.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
